rule.summary: German has several plural types: **-e**, **-(e)n**, **-er**, **-s** and **no ending**, often together with an umlaut (*a → ä, o → ö, u → ü, au → äu*). The plural cannot be fully predicted, so learn it with the noun (*der Tisch, -e*; *das Buch, ¨-er*). Gender gives useful tendencies. In the plural the article is always **die** (Nominativ and Akkusativ), the verb is plural, and in the Dativ the noun adds **-n** (*mit den Kindern*).
rule.table:
| Typ | Endung | Typisch für | Beispiele |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **-e** (oft mit Umlaut) | viele maskuline Nomen; einige neutrale; wenige einsilbige feminine | der Tag → die Tag**e**, der Stuhl → die St**ü**hl**e**, die Stadt → die St**ä**dt**e** |
| 2 | **-(e)n** | fast alle femininen Nomen; maskuline n-Deklination | die Frau → die Frau**en**, die Lampe → die Lampe**n**, der Kollege → die Kollege**n** |
| 3 | **-nen** | feminine Nomen auf *-in* | die Lehrerin → die Lehrerin**nen** |
| 4 | **-er** (mit Umlaut, wenn möglich) | viele einsilbige neutrale; wenige maskuline | das Kind → die Kind**er**, das Buch → die B**ü**ch**er**, der Mann → die M**ä**nn**er** |
| 5 | **–** (oft mit Umlaut) | maskuline und neutrale auf *-er, -el, -en*; *-chen, -lein* | der Lehrer → die Lehrer, der Apfel → die **Ä**pfel, das Mädchen → die Mädchen |
| 6 | **-s** | Wörter auf Vokal (nicht *-e*), viele Lehnwörter | das Auto → die Auto**s**, das Hotel → die Hotel**s**, das Handy → die Handy**s** |
steps: Learn every noun with article and plural: *der Tisch, -e*; *die Lampe, -n*; *das Buch, ¨-er*; *der Lehrer, -*.

If you do not know the plural, use the tendencies: feminine → **-(e)n** (*-in* → **-innen**); masculine → **-e**, often with umlaut; short neuter nouns → **-er** with umlaut; masculine/neuter in *-er, -el, -en* and all *-chen/-lein* → **no ending**; words ending in a vowel other than *-e* and many loans → **-s**.
Umlaut appears only with the types *-e*, *-er* and no ending. The *-(e)n* and *-s* plurals never add an umlaut.

Special endings: Latin *-um* and many Latin/Greek loans in *-a* → **-en** (*das Museum → die Museen, das Thema → die Themen*; but everyday words like *die Oma* take *-s*: *Omas*); *-nis* → **-nisse** (*das Ergebnis → die Ergebnisse*).
Use the plural article **die**, a plural verb (*Die Kinder spielen*), and after numbers above one and words like *viele, alle, beide* the plural form of the noun.
Dativ plural: article *den* + noun with **-n** (*den Kindern, den Männern*), unless the plural already ends in *-n* or *-s* (*den Frauen, den Autos*).
pitfalls: Forgetting the umlaut: ✗ *zwei Apfel, zwei Stuhle* → ✓ *zwei Äpfel, zwei Stühle*.
Using an English *-s*: ✗ *die Tischs, die Bananas* → ✓ *die Tische, die Bananen*.
Missing Dativ *-n*: ✗ *mit den Kinder* → ✓ *mit den Kindern*; but no extra *-n* in Nominativ/Akkusativ: ✗ *drei Kindern* (as object) → ✓ *drei Kinder*.
A singular verb with a plural noun: ✗ *Die Kinder spielt.* → ✓ *Die Kinder spielen.*

items.explanation: *der Mann* belongs to a small group of masculine nouns with the plural ending *-er*. With *-er* a back vowel takes an umlaut: a → ä → **Männer**. Most masculine nouns take *-e* instead (*Tage*), so learn *der Mann, ¨-er* as a unit.

mistake.why: The *-er* plural changes *a* to *ä* where possible. Without the umlaut the word is wrong: *Männer*.

items.explanation: Almost all feminine nouns form the plural with *-(e)n*. *Frau* does not end in *-e*, so it takes the full ending **-en**: Frau + en → **Frauen**. Plurals in *-(e)n* never take an umlaut.

mistake.why: *-s* is for loanwords and words ending in a vowel like *Auto*. A native feminine noun takes *-en*: *Frauen*.

items.explanation: Many short neuter nouns take **-er** in the plural: Kind + er → **Kinder**. The vowel *i* cannot take an umlaut, so only the ending changes.

mistake.why: German does not use the English *-s* here. *das Kind* is a short neuter noun with the plural *-er*: *Kinder*.

items.explanation: Most masculine nouns take **-e** in the plural: Hund + e → **Hunde**. Many of them also take an umlaut (*Stuhl → Stühle*), but not all: *Hund → Hunde*, *Tag → Tage*. The umlaut must be learned with the word.
items.pattern: der Hund → die Hund**e** (-e, ohne Umlaut)

mistake.why: *Hund* is one of the masculine nouns with *-e* but without an umlaut: *Hunde*.

items.explanation: Nouns that end in a vowel other than *-e* usually take **-s**: Auto + s → **Autos**, also *Kinos, Fotos, Omas*. The *-s* plural never has an umlaut.

mistake.why: After *zwei* the noun needs a plural form. *Auto* ends in *-o*, so the plural is *Autos*.

items.explanation: *das Buch* is a short neuter noun with the plural **-er**. With *-er* the vowel takes an umlaut wherever possible: u → ü → **Bücher**.

mistake.why: The *-er* plural always comes with an umlaut on *a, o, u, au*. So *u* becomes *ü*: *Bücher*.

items.explanation: Masculine nouns ending in *-el* get no plural ending. Here the plural is shown only by the umlaut: A → Ä → **Äpfel**. The article *die* and the plural verb also show the number.

mistake.why: Masculine *-el* nouns take no ending. The *-n* plural belongs to feminine *-el* nouns (*die Kartoffel → die Kartoffeln*). Correct: *Äpfel*.

items.explanation: Most feminine nouns take *-(e)n*, but a small group of one-syllable feminine nouns take umlaut + **-e**: *Stadt → **Städte***, also *Hand → Hände, Nacht → Nächte, Wand → Wände*. Note the spelling: *dt* stays.

mistake.why: *Stadt* does not follow the normal feminine *-en* pattern. It belongs to the small group with umlaut + *-e*: *Städte*.

items.explanation: *das Haus* takes the neuter plural **-er** with umlaut. The diphthong *au* becomes *äu*: Haus → **Häuser**. The pronunciation changes too: *äu* sounds like *eu*.

mistake.why: With the *-er* plural *au* changes to *äu*. Without the umlaut the form is wrong: *Häuser*.

items.explanation: Masculine and neuter nouns ending in *-er* take no plural ending: **Lehrer** stays the same. Only the article (*der → die*) and the verb show the plural: *Die Lehrer sind nett.*

mistake.why: Masculine nouns in *-er* add nothing in the plural. The English-style *-s* is wrong: *zwei Lehrer*.

items.en: One female teacher, two female teachers.
items.explanation: Feminine nouns in *-in* take the plural ending *-nen*, so the *n* is doubled: Lehrerin + nen → **Lehrerinnen**. The stress stays on the stem (*LEH-re-rin-nen*).

mistake.why: The *n* of *-in* is doubled in the plural: *-innen*. One *n* is a spelling and grammar mistake.

examples.en: One female doctor, two female doctors.
One female colleague, three female colleagues.

items.explanation: *der Tag* takes the typical masculine plural **-e**: Tag + e → **Tage**. It has no umlaut, although the vowel is *a* (compare *Stadt → Städte*). Time words often follow this pattern: *Monate, Abende*.
items.pattern: der Tag → die Tag**e** (-e, ohne Umlaut)

mistake.why: *Tag* has no umlaut in the plural. The form *Täge* does not exist: *sieben Tage*.

items.explanation: Feminine nouns that already end in *-e* add only **-n**: Banane + n → **Bananen**. This is the most regular plural in German.

mistake.why: *Bananas* is the English form. In German the feminine noun in *-e* adds *-n*: *Bananen*.

items.explanation: *viele* (many) is always followed by a plural noun. *Schule* is feminine and ends in *-e*, so it adds **-n**: **Schulen**.
items.pattern: viele + Plural: die Schule → die Schule**n**

mistake.why: *-s* is not used for native feminine nouns in *-e*. The plural is *Schulen*.

items.explanation: *der Stuhl* takes the masculine plural *-e* together with an umlaut: u → ü → **Stühle**. Many one-syllable masculine nouns work like this: *Zug → Züge, Platz → Plätze*.

mistake.why: *Stuhl* takes an umlaut in the plural: *Stühle*. Without it the form is wrong.

items.explanation: After a number above one the noun must be in the plural. *Lampe* is feminine in *-e* → **Lampen**. The *-n* plural has no umlaut, so the vowel *a* stays.
items.pattern: zwei + Plural: die Lampe → die Lampe**n**

mistake.why: After *zwei* the singular form is not possible. The noun needs its plural ending: *Lampen*.

items.explanation: Neuter nouns ending in *-er* take no plural ending and no umlaut: **Fenster** stays the same. In a sentence, the article *die* and the plural verb show the number: *Die Fenster sind offen.*

mistake.why: Neuter nouns in *-er* add nothing in the plural: *vier Fenster*.

items.explanation: *der Vogel* ends in *-el*, so it takes no ending; the plural is marked only by the umlaut o → ö → **Vögel**. Pronounce the *ö* clearly, because it is the only difference you can hear.

mistake.why: Without the umlaut, *Vogel* is singular. The plural needs *ö*: *Vögel*.

items.explanation: *Blume* is feminine in *-e* and adds **-n**: **Blumen**. The *-(e)n* plural never adds an umlaut, so *u* stays *u*.
items.pattern: die Blume → die Blume**n** (-n, kein Umlaut)

mistake.why: An umlaut only goes with the plural types *-e*, *-er* and no ending. With *-n* there is never an umlaut: *Blumen*.

items.explanation: Many loanwords from French and English keep the **-s** plural: Hotel + s → **Hotels**, also *Restaurants, Cafés*. The *-s* plural adds no umlaut and no extra *-n* in the Dativ (*in den Hotels*).

mistake.why: *Hotel* is a loanword and takes *-s*, not the native *-e*: *Hotels*.

items.en: The tables are made of wood.
items.explanation: *der Tisch* takes the common masculine plural **-e**, without umlaut (*i* cannot take one): **Tische**. The plural article *die* and the plural verb *sind* agree with it.

mistake.why: *-en* is the typical feminine plural. *Tisch* is masculine and takes *-e*: *die Tische*.

examples.en: The shoes are made of leather.
The rings are made of gold.

items.de: Zwei {{c1::Bücher::das Buch}} liegen auf dem Boden.
items.en: Two books are lying on the floor.
items.explanation: After *zwei* the noun is plural: *das Buch* → umlaut + *-er* → **Bücher**. The subject is plural, so the verb is plural too: *liegen*, not *liegt*.

mistake.wrong: Zwei Buch liegen auf dem Boden.
mistake.why: German, like English, needs the plural noun after a number above one: *zwei Bücher*.

examples.de: Zwei Gläser stehen auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: Two glasses are on the table.

examples.de: Drei Bilder hängen an der Wand.
examples.en: Three pictures are hanging on the wall.

items.en: The women work in the lab.
items.explanation: Feminine nouns usually take *-(e)n*: *die Frau → die **Frauen***. Because feminine singular and all plurals share the article *die*, the noun ending and the verb *arbeiten* are what show the plural here.

mistake.why: *die Frau* is singular and does not fit the plural verb *arbeiten*. With several women the noun is *Frauen*.

examples.en: The newspapers come in the morning.

items.en: All the rooms have a bathroom.
items.explanation: Masculine and neuter nouns in *-er, -el, -en* usually take no plural ending: *das Zimmer → die **Zimmer***. *alle* shows the plural. Careful: feminine nouns in *-er, -el* do take *-n* (*die Schwester → die Schwestern*).

mistake.why: The *-n* is added only in the Dativ plural (*in allen Zimmern*). As the subject the plural is just *Zimmer*.

examples.en: All the teachers are here today.

items.de: Die {{c1::Autos::das Auto}} stehen vor dem Haus.
items.en: The cars are parked in front of the house.
items.explanation: Nouns that end in a vowel other than *-e* take **-s**: *das Auto → die **Autos***. German uses *stehen* for parked cars, so the plural verb is *stehen*.

mistake.wrong: Die Auto stehen vor dem Haus.
mistake.why: *Auto* without *-s* is singular and does not match *die … stehen*. The plural is *Autos*.

examples.de: Die Kinos sind am Wochenende voll.
examples.en: The cinemas are full at the weekend.
The photos are hanging in the hall.

items.explanation: *das Kind* takes *-er* without umlaut: **Kinder** (compare *Buch → Bücher*). Here it is the Akkusativ object of *haben*, and in the Akkusativ plural the noun does not change.

mistake.why: *Kindern* is the Dativ plural (*mit den Kindern*). As the object of *haben* the form is *Kinder*.

items.de: Die {{c1::Städte::die Stadt}} im Süden sind wärmer.
items.en: The cities in the south are warmer.
items.explanation: *die Stadt* is one of the few feminine nouns with umlaut + *-e*: **Städte** (like *Hände, Nächte, Wände*). The plural subject takes the plural verb *sind*.

mistake.wrong: Die Stadte im Süden sind wärmer.
mistake.why: The ending *-e* is right, but the umlaut is missing: *a* must become *ä* → *Städte*.

examples.de: Die Nächte im Sommer sind kurz.
examples.en: The nights in summer are short.

examples.de: Die Wände im Bad sind weiß.
examples.en: The walls in the bathroom are white.

items.en: My female friends are coming later.
items.explanation: Nouns in *-in* double the *n* and add *-en*: *die Freundin → die **Freundinnen***. The possessive *meine* has the plural ending *-e*, and the verb *kommen* is plural.

mistake.why: German does not use *-s* for nouns in *-in*. The plural ending is *-nen*: *Freundinnen*.

examples.en: My female colleagues are very nice.
Her female neighbours often help her.

items.explanation: Some masculine nouns take **only an umlaut** in the plural: *der Apfel → die **Äpfel***. In speech, *die Äpfel* and *der Apfel* differ only in the article and the first vowel, so the plural verb *sind* helps.

mistake.why: Without the umlaut the noun is singular. With *die … sind* it must be the plural *Äpfel*.

examples.de: Die Gärten sind im Frühling schön.
examples.en: The gardens are beautiful in spring.

examples.de: Die Väter spielen mit den Kindern.
examples.en: The fathers are playing with the children.

items.explanation: *beide* (both) is always followed by a plural noun. *das Haus* takes the classic neuter pattern umlaut + *-er*: **Häuser**. The verb *wurden* is plural too.

mistake.why: *beide* means two things, so the noun must be plural: *beide Häuser*.

items.en: The countries are signing the treaty.
items.explanation: *das Land* takes umlaut + *-er*: **Länder**. In the Dativ plural an *-n* is added: *in vielen Ländern*. Here *die Länder* is the subject, so there is no *-n*.

mistake.why: *das Land* takes the plural *-er* with umlaut, not *-e*: *die Länder*.

examples.de: Die Dörfer liegen in den Bergen.
examples.en: The villages are in the mountains.

examples.de: Die Wörter stehen an der Tafel.
examples.en: The words are on the board.

items.explanation: *die Idee* already ends in *-e*, so the plural adds only **-n**: **Ideen**. It is pronounced with three syllables: *I-de-en*. As the object of *mögen* it is Akkusativ plural, which looks the same as the Nominativ.

mistake.why: *Idee* is feminine and ends in *-e*, so it takes *-n*, not *-s*: *Ideen*.

items.explanation: *der Mann* belongs to the small group of masculine nouns with umlaut + *-er*: **Männer** (also *Wälder, Götter, Geister*). The plural subject takes the plural verb *warten*.

mistake.why: German does not use the *-s* plural for *Mann*. The plural is *Männer*.

examples.de: Die Wälder sind im Herbst bunt.
examples.en: The forests are colourful in autumn.

examples.de: Die Geister im Film sind lustig.
examples.en: The ghosts in the film are funny.

items.explanation: English loans keep the **-s** plural in German, and words in *-y* simply add *-s*: **Handys**, *Babys, Hobbys*. The English spelling *-ies* is not used in German.

mistake.why: German does not change *-y* to *-ies*. The plural is *Handys*.

examples.en: Two babies are sleeping in the room.

items.en: The doctors are taking a break.
items.explanation: *der Arzt* takes the masculine plural umlaut + *-e*: a → ä → **Ärzte**. The female form has a different plural: *die Ärztin → die Ärztinnen*.

mistake.why: The ending *-e* is right, but *Arzt* also needs the umlaut: *Ärzte*.

examples.en: The balls are in the garden.

examples.de: Die Köche arbeiten in der Küche.
examples.en: The cooks are working in the kitchen.

items.en: All the students get an email.
items.explanation: *der Student* is an n-Deklination noun: it takes **-en** in the plural and in every singular case except the Nominativ (*den Studenten*). So the plural is **Studenten**, like *Touristen, Praktikanten*.

mistake.why: The English *-s* is wrong. *Student* is an n-Deklination noun with the plural *Studenten*.

examples.en: All the interns get a laptop.
The tourists are taking photos of the cathedral.

items.de: Die {{c1::Busse::der Bus}} kommen heute zu spät.
items.explanation: *der Bus* takes the masculine plural *-e*. After the short vowel *u* the *s* is doubled so the vowel stays short: Bus + s + e → **Busse**. The verb *kommen* is plural.

mistake.wrong: Die Buse kommen heute zu spät.
mistake.why: With a single *s* the *u* would be long. The *s* is doubled: *Busse*.

items.de: Ich habe zwei {{c1::Brüder::der Bruder}} und eine Schwester.
items.en: I have two brothers and a sister.
items.explanation: *der Bruder* ends in *-er*, so it takes no plural ending, but it does take an umlaut: u → ü → **Brüder**. Compare the feminine *die Schwester*, which takes *-n*: *die Schwestern*.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe zwei Bruder und eine Schwester.
mistake.why: *Bruder* without umlaut is singular. After *zwei* the plural *Brüder* is needed.

examples.de: Sie hat zwei Schwestern und einen Bruder.
examples.en: She has two sisters and a brother.

items.explanation: Feminine nouns normally take *-(e)n*, but *die Tochter* and *die Mutter* form the plural with **only an umlaut**: o → ö → **Töchter**, *Mütter*. These two words must be learned as exceptions.

mistake.why: *Tochter* does not follow the usual feminine *-n* pattern (unlike *Schwestern*). Its plural is *Töchter*.

examples.de: Die Mütter treffen sich im Park.
examples.en: The mothers meet in the park.
Our mothers know each other well.

items.de: Wir spielen mit den {{c1::Kindern::das Kind → Dat. Pl.}} im Park.
items.en: We play with the children in the park.
items.explanation: *mit* always takes the Dativ. In the Dativ plural the article is *den* and the noun adds **-n**: Kinder + n → **Kindern**. This *-n* is added to every plural that does not already end in *-n* or *-s*.

mistake.wrong: Wir spielen mit den Kinder im Park.
mistake.why: In the Dativ plural the noun needs *-n*: *mit den Kindern*.

examples.de: Wir fahren mit den Fahrrädern zur Arbeit.
examples.en: We go to work by bike.

items.en: The museums are closed on Mondays.
items.explanation: Latin loans in *-um* replace *-um* with **-en**: Muse(um) → **Museen**, *Zentrum → Zentren*. The ending is not added to the full word; it replaces the last syllable.

mistake.why: Words in *-um* do not take *-s*. The *-um* is replaced by *-en*: *Museen*.

examples.de: Die Zentren der Städte sind am Abend voll.
examples.en: The city centres are full in the evening.

examples.de: Die Gymnasien in der Stadt sind sehr gut.
examples.en: The grammar schools in the city are very good.

items.explanation: Nouns in *-nis* take the plural *-e* and double the *s*: Ergebnis + s + e → **Ergebnisse**. The same happens with *das Zeugnis → die Zeugnisse*.

mistake.why: The *s* of *-nis* is doubled in the plural: *Ergebnisse*.

examples.en: The school reports come in July.

examples.de: Die Erlebnisse im Urlaub waren toll.
examples.en: The experiences on holiday were great.

items.explanation: Nouns in *-chen* and *-lein* never change in the plural: **Mädchen** stays the same. Here only the article *die* (instead of *das*) and the plural verb *spielen* show that there are several girls.

mistake.why: *-chen* nouns add nothing in the plural, also not *-s*: *die Mädchen*.

examples.en: The bread rolls are still warm.
The kittens are sleeping in the basket.

items.de: Die {{c1::Wohnungen::die Wohnung}} hier sind sehr teuer.
items.en: The flats here are very expensive.
items.explanation: Every noun in *-ung* is feminine and takes **-en** in the plural: Wohnung + en → **Wohnungen**. This rule has no exceptions, so it is a safe pattern.

mistake.wrong: Die Wohnung hier sind sehr teuer.
mistake.why: *Wohnung* is singular and does not match *sind*. The plural is *Wohnungen*.

examples.de: Die Rechnungen liegen auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The bills are on the table.

items.en: I'm buying a kilo of potatoes.
items.explanation: Feminine nouns in *-el* add **-n**: Kartoffel + n → **Kartoffeln** (unlike masculine *Äpfel*). After a quantity like *ein Kilo*, countable things stand in the plural, without *of*: *ein Kilo Kartoffeln*.
items.pattern: Menge + Nomen (Pl.): die Kartoffel → die Kartoffel**n**

mistake.why: A kilo contains many potatoes, so the noun is plural. Feminine *-el* nouns add *-n*: *Kartoffeln*.

examples.en: I'm buying a kilo of onions.
We need two kilos of tomatoes.

items.explanation: Masculine nouns in *-e* for people or animals (*der Kollege, der Junge, der Kunde*) belong to the n-Deklination and add **-n** in the plural: **Kollegen**. So not every masculine noun takes *-e*; these take *-n*.

mistake.why: *Kollege* is singular. In the plural it takes *-n*: *die Kollegen*.

examples.de: Die Kunden warten an der Kasse.
examples.en: The customers are waiting at the till.

items.de: Die {{c1::Themen::das Thema}} im Kurs sind interessant.
items.en: The topics in the course are interesting.
items.explanation: Many loans in *-a* replace the *-a* with **-en**: Them(a) → **Themen**, *die Firma → die Firmen*. The final vowel disappears; the ending is not just added.

mistake.wrong: Die Themas im Kurs sind interessant.
mistake.why: In standard German the plural of *Thema* is *Themen*. The *-a* is replaced by *-en*.

examples.en: The companies are looking for new employees.

examples.de: Die Villen am See sind teuer.
examples.en: The villas by the lake are expensive.

items.de: Die {{c1::Leute::people (nur Plural)}} hier sind sehr freundlich.
items.en: The people here are very friendly.
items.explanation: *die Leute* exists only in the plural; there is no singular form (for one person you say *die Person* or *der Mensch*). So the verb is always plural: *Die Leute sind …*.

mistake.wrong: Die Leuten hier sind sehr freundlich.
mistake.why: *Leuten* is the Dativ form (*mit den Leuten*). As the subject the form is *Leute*.

examples.en: The school holidays start in July.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about plural tendencies.
drills.prompt: Which plural ending is most typical for each gender?
drills.answer: **Feminine** → *-(e)n* (*-in* → *-innen*). **Masculine** → *-e*, often with umlaut. **Neuter** (short words) → *-er* with umlaut; other neuter nouns often *-e*. Masculine and neuter nouns in *-er, -el, -en* → **no ending**.
drills.explanation: These are tendencies, not rules: *die Stadt → die Städte* and *der Mann → die Männer* are exceptions. The plural must still be learned with each noun.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the -s plural.
drills.prompt: Which nouns take the plural ending -s?
drills.answer: Nouns that end in a vowel other than *-e* (*Autos, Kinos, Omas*), many English and French loans (*Hotels, Handys, Restaurants*), and short forms (*die LKWs, die Unis*).
drills.explanation: *-s* is a small group in German, unlike English. It never adds an umlaut and never gets an extra Dativ *-n* (*mit den Autos*). Native German nouns almost never use it.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the Dativ plural.
drills.prompt: What changes in the Dativ plural?
drills.answer: The article is **den**, and the noun adds **-n**: *die Kinder → mit den Kinder**n***. No *-n* is added when the plural already ends in *-n* or *-s*: *mit den Frauen, mit den Autos*.
drills.explanation: Nominativ and Akkusativ plural look the same (*die Kinder*). Only the Dativ has its own noun ending. This is one of the most frequent mistakes in writing.

examples.de: Er gibt den Gästen das Essen.
examples.en: He serves the guests the food.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the umlaut in the plural.
drills.prompt: With which plural types can an umlaut appear, and with which never?
drills.answer: Possible with **-e** (*Stühle*), **-er** (*Bücher*, always if the vowel allows it) and **no ending** (*Äpfel*). Never with **-(e)n** (*Blumen*) or **-s** (*Autos*).
drills.explanation: With *-er* the umlaut is automatic on *a, o, u, au*. With *-e* and no ending it depends on the word (*Tage* but *Stühle*). So when you learn a plural, notice whether it has an umlaut.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about nouns with only one number.
drills.prompt: Name some nouns that exist only in the plural, and some that are normally used only in the singular.
drills.answer: Only plural: **die Leute, die Eltern, die Geschwister, die Ferien**. Normally only singular: **das Obst, das Gemüse, die Milch, der Zucker, das Geld**.
drills.explanation: English sometimes differs: *vegetables* is plural, but *das Gemüse* is singular (*Das Gemüse ist frisch.*). *die Ferien* is plural, so the verb is plural: *Die Ferien sind vorbei.*

drills.instruction: Choose the correct plural form.
drills.answer: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.
drills.explanation: *die Schwester* is feminine, and feminine nouns in *-er* take *-n*: *Schwestern*. *Schwester* is singular and wrong after *zwei*; *Schwesters* uses the English *-s*.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct plural form.
drills.answer: Auf dem Tisch liegen zwei Messer.
drills.explanation: *das Messer* is neuter in *-er*, so the plural has no ending: *Messer*. *Messers* is the Genitiv singular, and *Messern* is the Dativ plural, but here the knives are the subject.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct form.
drills.answer: Die Lehrerin hilft den Schülern.
drills.explanation: *helfen* takes the Dativ, and *den* here is the Dativ plural. The plural *Schüler* adds the Dativ *-n*: *Schülern*. *Schüler* lacks the *-n*, and *Schülers* is a Genitiv singular form.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct plural form.
drills.prompt: In der Stadt gibt es viele ___.
drills.answer: In der Stadt gibt es viele Cafés.
drills.explanation: *das Café* is a French loan ending in a vowel, so it takes *-s*: *Cafés*. The native endings *-en* and *-er* are not used with this word.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.answer: Ich habe zwei Kinder.
drills.explanation: The mistake: after *zwei* the noun must be plural. *das Kind* takes *-er*: *zwei Kinder*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.answer: Die Kinder spielen im Garten.
drills.explanation: The mistake is the verb. *Die Kinder* is plural, so the verb must be plural: *spielen*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.prompt: Wir fahren mit unseren Freunde nach Wien.
drills.answer: Wir fahren mit unseren Freunden nach Wien.
drills.explanation: The mistake is the missing Dativ *-n*. *mit* takes the Dativ, and in the Dativ plural *Freunde* becomes *Freunden*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.answer: Ich kaufe drei Äpfel.
drills.explanation: The mistake is the missing umlaut. *der Apfel* takes no plural ending, so the umlaut is the only plural signal: *Äpfel*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.answer: Die Lehrerinnen sind sehr nett.
drills.explanation: The mistake: nouns in *-in* double the *n* in the plural. The correct form is *Lehrerinnen*.

drills.instruction: Make the subject plural. Change the verb.
drills.answer: Die Bücher sind teuer.
drills.explanation: *das* becomes *die*, *Buch* takes umlaut + *-er* → *Bücher*, and *ist* becomes *sind*. The adjective after *sein* does not change.

drills.instruction: Make the subject plural. Change the verb.
drills.answer: Die Züge haben Verspätung.
drills.explanation: *der Zug* takes umlaut + *-e* → *die Züge*, and the verb changes from *hat* to *haben*. *Verspätung* stays singular; it is the delay, not the trains.

drills.instruction: Make the subject plural. Change the verb.
drills.answer: Die Studentinnen wohnen in Köln.
drills.explanation: The article stays *die*, because feminine singular and plural share it. *Studentin* takes *-nen* → *Studentinnen*, and the verb becomes *wohnen*.

drills.instruction: Replace *ein* with *zwei*. Change the noun.
drills.answer: Ich brauche zwei Gläser.
drills.explanation: After *zwei* the noun must be plural. *das Glas* is a short neuter noun with umlaut + *-er*: *Gläser*. It is the Akkusativ object, so no Dativ *-n* is added.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order. Start with: Die
drills.prompt: auf dem Tisch / liegen / Zeitungen / die
drills.answer: Die Zeitungen liegen auf dem Tisch.
drills.explanation: The plural subject *Die Zeitungen* (*die Zeitung, -en*) is in position 1, the plural verb *liegen* in position 2, and the place follows. Another correct order: *Auf dem Tisch liegen die Zeitungen.*

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order. Start with: In Berlin
drills.prompt: gibt / viele / es / Parks / in Berlin
drills.answer: In Berlin gibt es viele Parks.
drills.explanation: *In Berlin* is in position 1, so the verb *gibt* follows and then *es*. *der Park* is a loan with the plural *-s*: *viele Parks*. Another correct order: *Es gibt viele Parks in Berlin.*
